prize_parts.citation: for the theoretical prediction of flat bands in magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states in it

statement.case_for: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene is the cleanest recent case in condensed matter of a sharp theoretical prediction (the Bistritzer-MacDonald continuum model of 2011, with flat bands at a specific twist angle) followed by an unambiguous experimental discovery (correlated insulators and gate-tunable superconductivity in 2018) in a single carbon-based material. The twist angle as a continuous design parameter created moire quantum materials as a field, with many independent replications across graphene, TMD and other platforms within a few years. It is original, can be stated in one sentence, and the eight openings put it first for three members and in the top four for four. Having re-read the openings, I now think the theory-plus-experiment trio that most colleagues propose is the better-defended configuration than my own opening choice.
statement.case_against: The microscopic pairing mechanism of the superconductivity is still unsettled, and twist-angle disorder makes sample-to-sample reproducibility uneven, so a skeptic can say the field is about eight years old and still moving fast. The three-name cap also forces Eva Andrei, whose early scanning-probe evidence of flat bands and van Hove singularities at small twist angles is a genuine experimental contribution, out of the configuration, and I cannot settle her weight against the others from the supplied evidence alone. A prize that leaves her out risks looking arbitrary in hindsight.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks B025 first as a theory prediction followed by experimental demonstration, notes that leaving out Andrei is a real allocation difficulty, and proposes MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero and Bistritzer as a coherent three.
responses.response: I agree on the structure and I move toward your trio. In my opening I put Andrei in place of Bistritzer, but your argument and the fact that seven of eight openings name Bistritzer make me weigh the 2011 continuum model more heavily: without it there is no magic angle to look for, and the 2018 experiments were explicitly motivated by it. Where I would qualify your view is that Andrei's contribution should not be treated as trivial. It is earlier experimental evidence that the physics was real, and I want the citation worded so that it does not imply that nobody had seen flat-band signatures before 2018.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks the topological-insulator line B033 first and B025 second, saying that B025 is early because the superconductivity mechanism is unresolved and that Andrei's competing claim cannot be settled from the supplied evidence.
responses.response: I take the maturity worry seriously but I do not think it should decide the matter. The Nobel criterion is the discovery of the phenomena, not the explanation of every mechanism: the existence of correlated insulators and superconductivity at the magic angle is secure and has been reproduced by many groups, as you also concede. I also disagree that B033 should displace B013, because bundling the quantum anomalous Hall effect with the quantum spin Hall effect makes a compound prize with three experimental threads, whereas B025 is one discovery. On Andrei I share your uncertainty, and I list it among my unresolved points rather than pretend it is resolved.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks optical lattice clocks B006 first as a clean, mature, timely instrument-plus-concept prize, and places the twisted-bilayer-graphene entry sixth because the field is young and the superconductivity mechanism is unsettled.
responses.response: The clock case is strong, and that is why I name B006 as an alternative: the magic-wavelength idea is original, the 1e-18 results are reproduced by several national laboratories, and the redefinition of the second makes the timing good. Where I disagree is on the weight of youth. Eight years with wide independent replication and a whole subfield is not premature by the standard of earlier prizes, and I do not think the 2005 and 2012 prizes in frequency metrology and ion clocks leave a clock prize wholly free of overlap, which is the same kind of closeness we hold against B009. I would accept B006 as a fair outcome but not as clearly stronger than B025.

responses.point: Kroll ranks B006 first and B025 sixth, calling the allocation 'a fair three but leaves a notable name out' and the timing probably early because the interpretation of the superconductivity is still debated.
responses.response: We agree that the omission of Andrei is the weak point, and I do not dismiss it. But 'probably early' needs a standard: the phenomenon itself, correlated insulating states and superconductivity tuned by gate voltage at the magic angle, has been seen by many groups in several moire systems, which is more than the replication that preceded several recent prizes. I would be more persuaded by your timing concern if there were conflicting experimental results, and what we have instead is an open theoretical question about pairing.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks B025 first, says the Bistritzer-MacDonald prediction and the 2018 Jarillo-Herrero experiments are the decisive pair, and finds the timing ripe, while noting that Andrei's early work makes a three-person prize built on prediction plus discovery the cleaner configuration.
responses.response: I agree with the core of your reading and with the timing, and my revised configuration follows it. I would add a caution about 'cleaner': a configuration is cleaner for the committee but not necessarily more accurate historically, and I would want the final citation to name the prediction and the discovery rather than imply a single origin. I also differ from you a little on B013, which you rank second: I place it second as well, but the missing Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang credit and the 2D/3D split with Hasan leave it with a messier attribution than B025.

uncertainties: Whether Andrei's early scanning-probe work deserves a place in the three-name set instead of Bistritzer or MacDonald; I rely on my memory of the historical record rather than on supplied verification.
Whether the unresolved pairing mechanism of the superconductivity should delay recognition, or whether the discovery of the phenomena is enough.
Whether the 2025 superconducting-circuit prize makes any further recognition of superconducting-circuit physics (B009) imprudent for several years, which is why I do not put it first.
Whether B013 would be better framed with Hasan or the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang theory credited, given that those names are outside or at the margin of the supplied set.
statement.conflict_note: I direct the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology and work in circuit QED and waveguide QED at Chalmers, so B009 (circuit quantum electrodynamics) is in my own subfield and I should not argue for it; I have deliberately not put it in my preferred configuration or alternatives. Chalmers colleagues Per Delsing and C. M. Wilson, my frequent co-author Anton Frisk Kockum and the WACQT groups are documented connections to the superconducting-circuit area. No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for B025, B013 or B006.
